procedural_history.impugned_order: Order of acquittal of the appellants for an offence under Section 7(1) read with Sections 16 and 17 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The State of Maharashtra appealed the acquittal to the High Court of Bombay (Aurangabad Bench) in Criminal Appeal No. 90 of 1983. A Single Judge of the High Court heard the appeal, allowed it, held the appellants guilty, and set aside the order of acquittal. This was done on June 13, 1986.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellants appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave, arguing that the High Court appeal should have been heard by a Division Bench, not a Single Judge, according to the Bombay High Court Appellate Side Rules, 1960. The Supreme Court agreed, allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court's order, and remanded the matter to the High Court to be heard by a Division Bench.

directions: Send the matter back to the High Court for being placed before a Division Bench of the High Court.
The Division Bench will afford reasonable opportunity of hearing to both the sides and dispose it of in accordance with law, expeditiously.

issue.issue_text: Whether a judgment delivered by a Single Judge of the High Court is a nullity when the relevant High Court rules require the matter to be heard and decided by a Division Bench.

facts: An appeal against an acquittal for an offense punishable with more than two years of imprisonment was heard and decided by a Single Judge of the High Court.
Under the relevant Bombay High Court Appellate Side Rules, 1960 (specifically Rule 1 and Rule 2-II(e)), such an appeal was required to be heard by a Division Bench, consisting of at least two judges.
law: A court or judge must have the legal competence and jurisdiction to hear and decide a matter.

The Bombay High Court Appellate Side Rules, 1960, mandate that certain appeals, including those against acquittals for offenses punishable with more than two years imprisonment, must be heard by a Division Bench.
application: The Supreme Court reasoned that when the rules explicitly require a matter to be heard by a Division Bench, a Single Judge lacks the legal competence or jurisdiction to decide it.
This is not a mere procedural irregularity but a "total lack of jurisdiction."
The Court emphasized that the merits of the decision are irrelevant, stating, "Even a 'right' decision by a 'wrong' forum is no decision. It is non-existent in the eye of law."
The accused had a right to be heard by two judges as per the rules, and this right cannot be taken away without amending those rules.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the judgment delivered by the Single Judge was a nullity because the judge lacked the jurisdiction to hear the case. The Court set aside the judgment and remanded the matter to the High Court to be heard by a proper Division Bench.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a judgment delivered by a Single Judge of the High Court is a nullity when the relevant High Court rules require the matter to be heard and decided by a Division Bench.
appellant_arguments: The appeal against acquittal was required to be heard by a Division Bench under the Bombay High Court Appellate Side Rules 1960, as the offence was punishable with a sentence of imprisonment exceeding two years.
The accused has a right to be heard by at least two judges, and this right cannot be taken away unless the rules are amended.
Denying this right is arbitrary and discriminatory, and the error cannot be cured or excused by claiming it was due to negligence.
A decision made by a forum that lacks competence over the subject matter is not a real decision in the eyes of the law; it is a nullity.
Even a correct decision on the merits is invalid if delivered by the wrong forum.

cases.case_name: State of Madhya Pradesh v. Dewadas & Ors.
cases.principle: To reinforce the view that a judgment rendered by a forum that lacks jurisdiction under the rules (a Single Judge instead of a Division Bench) is a nullity and must be set aside.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A judgment rendered by a Single Judge in a matter that, according to procedural rules, must be heard by a Division Bench is a nullity, as it is a decision from a forum that lacks the jurisdiction to hear the case. A litigant's right to be heard by the proper forum is absolute and cannot be nullified by administrative negligence or error.
obiter: The Registry of the High Court was expected to have realized the true position and ought not to have created a situation which resulted in waste of court time.
No Court can afford this luxury with the mountain of arrears which every Court is carrying these days.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: When a matter required to be decided by a Division Bench of the High Court is decided by a learned Single Judge, the judgment is a nullity. The matter was heard by a court which had no competence, which constitutes a total lack of jurisdiction. Even a 'right' decision by a 'wrong' forum is no decision; it is non-existent in the eye of law.
legal_tests_applied: Whether a judgment is valid is determined by whether the forum that delivered it had the competence and jurisdiction to hear the subject matter as prescribed by the relevant procedural rules. A decision rendered by a forum lacking such competence is a nullity, regardless of its correctness on the merits.
why_appellant_lost: The provided text does not contain reasoning for the appellant losing, as the appellant's appeal was allowed by the court.
why_respondent_won: The accused had a right under the Bombay High Court Appellate Side Rules, 1960, to be heard by at least two judges constituting a Division Bench, as the offence was punishable with imprisonment exceeding two years.
This right cannot be taken away except by amending the rules, and to deny this right is arbitrary and discriminatory.
A judgment delivered by a forum that lacks competence over the subject matter is a nullity, even if the decision is correct on the merits.
The matter having been heard by a Single Judge instead of a Division Bench was a matter of total lack of jurisdiction, not a mere irregularity.
The error could not be excused by claiming it was due to negligence, as negligence cannot cure the infirmity or illegality or rob the accused of their right under the rules.
policy_considerations: The court noted that the registry's error resulted in a 'waste of court time,' a luxury no court can afford 'with the mountain of arrears which every Court is carrying these days.'
Upholding the rules regarding the composition of benches is essential to avoid arbitrary and discriminatory denial of procedural rights to an accused.
